newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Arafat criticises Israel at Islamic summit.
newsitem.headline: Arafat criticises Israel at Islamic summit.

text.p: Islamic leaders met for a special summit conference to mark Pakistan's golden jubilee on Sunday and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat used the occasion to attack what he called Israeli aggression in the Middle East.
The one-day summit of the 54-member Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) in Islamabad was called to help Pakistan mark its golden jubilee year, celebrating 50 years of independence.
It took place in a round convention centre built for the occasion. Ousted Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, who persuaded the OIC in 1995 to hold the summit, was not there.
Arafat told the meeting that Israeli "obstinacy and intransigence" had frozen peace negotiations with Syria and Lebanon and was hindering those with the Palestinians.
"We were surprised by the Israeli decision to isolate and Judaise Jerusalem, constructing new settlements not only inside it but outside it," Arafat said.

Israeli-Palestinian tension has been high since right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent bulldozers last Tuesday to a hill in Arab East Jerusalem to begin building a new Jewish settlement in territory occupied by Israel.
A suicide bombing, claimed by the radical Moslem group Hamas, killed three Israeli women in Tel Aviv on Friday.
Arafat accused Israel of delaying implementation of agreements with the Palestinians to "please right-wing Israeli religious parties which are hostile to the peace process".
Speaking for the Arab group at the OIC, Arafat criticised the United States for vetoing a U.N. Security Council resolution demanding that Israel halt the East Jerusalem settlement.
"Unfortunately the veto of the United States, twice, only helped encourage Israel to pursue its aggression and its challenge to international legitimacy," Arafat said.
Pakistani President Farooq Leghari, in his inaugural speech, said his country wanted good relations with its arch-rival India, but their dispute over Kashmir must be solved.
"A just solution of the Kashmir dispute, in accordance with U.N. resolutions, is essential to ease tensions which have afflicted relations between Indian and Pakistan," Leghari said.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif also spoke of the need for an "honourable settlement" of the Kashmir dispute.
"We have decided to resume bilateral talks with India in the hope that India would reciprocate this gesture," he said.
The top officials of the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministries are due to meet in New Delhi from March 28 to 31 to renew a dialogue that foundered over Kashmir in January 1994.
Earlier Islamic leaders watched a military parade through Islamabad as airforce jets screamed overhead in formation.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and Arafat were the most prominent leaders watching the parade.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Abdullah and Bangladesh's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, the only woman leader to attend, were also there, but most Arab heads of state stayed away.
